query: For rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs a strong magnetocaloric response at low applied fields while maintaining rapid heat exchange, low hysteresis, and mechanical stability? State one controlled intervention that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that would support it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A nanoscale dual-phase microstructure, engineered by introducing controlled secondary phase precipitates within a ferromagnetic matrix, enhances the magnetocaloric response at low applied fields by locally modulating exchange interactions while preserving rapid heat transfer and low hysteresis.
generation.material_initial_state: A rare-earth-free high-entropy alloy initially synthesized as a predominantly single-phase ferromagnetic material.
generation.intervention: Induce 5–10% volume fraction of nanoscale secondary phase precipitates by controlled rapid solidification (or additive manufacturing) followed by a heat treatment at 700–750 °C for 30 minutes to achieve precipitate sizes of 10–20 nm.
generation.conditions: Samples must have identical alloy compositions and controlled cooling rates, with heat treatment performed under inert conditions; testing is carried out under low-field (<5 T) magnetic conditions and relevant refrigeration temperature ranges.
generation.structural_mediator: An engineered dual-phase structure where soft ferromagnetic domains coexist with uniformly dispersed nanoscale precipitates, which modulate local exchange interactions.
generation.mechanism: The nanoscale precipitates serve as nucleation sites for localized spin reorientation, facilitating a higher magnetic entropy change at low fields. Their sub-20 nm size minimizes domain wall pinning and hysteresis while the dual-phase network maintains effective heat exchange and mechanical stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a single-phase baseline, the dual-phase alloy will display a significantly enhanced ΔSm, reduced coercivity and hysteresis losses, and retain dynamic thermal response and mechanical robustness.
generation.baseline: The identical alloy processed to remain nearly single-phase without deliberate secondary phase precipitate formation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is applicable to high-entropy alloys based on 3d transition metals where controlled secondary phase formation is feasible, and under operating temperatures relevant for magnetic refrigeration with applied fields up to 5 T.
generation.uncertainty: Exact optimization of secondary phase volume fraction and uniform dispersion remains challenging; processing variations may require further calibration to avoid mechanical degradation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two groups: one processed via rapid solidification plus the defined heat treatment to produce 5–10% nanoscale precipitates, and one processed to achieve a single-phase structure. Characterize precipitate size and distribution using TEM and compare magnetocaloric properties, coercivity, and hysteresis between the two groups.
measurements: Magnetic entropy change (ΔSm) determination from M–T curves
High-resolution TEM/EDX for precipitate identification and quantification
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dual-phase samples do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in magnetocaloric performance and reduced hysteresis relative to the single-phase control, the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Delving deeper, unfortunately, RCP tends to overestimate the merits of the materials which have a large temperature range of magnetocaloric effect (δTFWHM) but small entropy changes [,] in no small part because materials with same relative cooling power can behave differently in a magnetic cooling simulation []. Moreover, one of the last printed books about magnetic cooling ignores this figure of merit []. In order to be of use in magnetic refrigeration applications the chosen materials have to show a large magnetocaloric effect—a large magnetic entropy change. Besides this, there is a list of requirements related with heat transfer, heat capacity, heat conductivity, chemical and mechanical stability, hysteresis losses, eddy currents losses, etc. Therefore, magnetic measurements can be a trusted guide in deciding if a material deserves the effort of complete characterization. Some compounds of the type A1−xBxMnO3 can be considered to be of interest for magnetic refrigeration because some of these compounds show −ΔSm values (−ΔSm ≈ 4–6 J·kg−1·K−1 for ΔH = 5 T) comparable to intermetallic alloys []. This is the case of our investigated compounds.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) were initially proposed for simple crystal structures such as face-centered cubic (fcc), body-centered cubic (bcc), and hexagonal close packing (hcp), in which more than five elements, each having an atomic fraction between 5% and 35%, randomly occupy one crystallographic site [,]. The HEA concept is now adopted in various crystal structures [,]. The high-entropy state contributes to the stability of the solid solution with the desired crystal structure through the relatively large mixing entropy. For example, (Gd1/6Tb1/6Dy1/6Tm1/6Yb1/6Lu1/6)2Si2O7 disilicate shows outstanding thermal stability, which is ascribed to the high-entropy state at the rare-earth site []. The significant atomic disorder leads to the severe lattice distortion effect. In particular, bcc HEAs show superior mechanical properties, attracting a great deal of interest. There is also growing interest in the study of HEAs with high ductility, refractory HEAs, those demonstrating superconductivity, as well as HEAs used in anti-corrosion coatings, biomaterials, catalysts, shape memory alloys, magnetic refrigeration materials, and so on [,,,,,,,,,].
